headline: Bay Anchovies Flood the Boulder Fields — Albies Riding the Tide Right Behind Them
subhead: Fishers Island Sound's rock piles are loaded with bait, the first albies are pushing through the Race, and the moon says the real blitz is still a few days out.
body_markdown:
The boulder fields between Wamphassuc Point and Ram Island have been carrying bait for about ten days now — not peanut bunker, not silversides, but the tight little clouds of bay anchovies that push into these rock piles every September and turn the whole Sound into a feeding lane. You can see them from the surface on a calm morning, a smoky shadow drifting across the granite, and where that shadow slows down and balls up tight against structure, that's where something's usually working underneath it.

We flagged this last week — said bonito numbers would build in this corridor as fish worked west out of Rhode Island and Buzzards Bay, and that's exactly what's happening. Bonito are showing off the east side of Fishers Island and along the Watch Hill breakwater riprap, mixed in loosely with the first real numbers of false albacore. Neither fish has committed to a full-blown blitz yet — this is still feeder behavior, small pods surfacing for thirty seconds and disappearing, not the sustained peeling-drag runs we'll get once the water cools another few degrees and the moon does its work. New London is reading 69.4 that's warm enough to hold both species comfortably, and the full moon that just passed on the 6th and 7th should have tightened those anchovy schools further. The next real trigger is the new moon on the 10th — historically that's when this stretch of the Sound flips from scattered surface activity to fish up and thrashing for an hour at a stretch.

Because the bait right now is anchovy-sized — an inch, inch and a half — the albies have been picky about profile. Standard 3-inch epoxy jigs are getting refused more than they're getting hit. The better producers this week have been the smaller stuff: 1/2-ounce Deadly Dicks in bone or chartreuse, half-ounce Albie Snax, and on the fly side, size 2 Clouser minimolls or a slim epoxy pattern on a 9-weight with a straight 20-pound fluoro leader. Bonito have been a little less fussy and will still eat a Point Judith Swedish Pimple or a small metal worked fast through a rip. The key with both fish right now is speed and location — cast into the boil, not ahead of it, because these schools are moving and gone in seconds around the rocks off Ram Island and the eastern face of the Stonington breakwater.

Striped bass are still mostly a bunker story. Watch Hill Reef has had bunker schools stacked tight for a couple weeks, and the bass working underneath them have been a mix of school fish and a few better ones in the 28 to 34-inch range, taken on live bunker fished on a fish-finder rig right down into the pods, or on bunker spoons trolled slow along the reef's edge on the last of the ebb. That bunker-bass pattern coastwide is supposedly tightening under this moon, and if that holds, the next push of bass ought to start showing real interest rather than just picking at stragglers — which is the stage we're seeing right now in this zone. The boulder field game for stripers has been slower and more technical: paddle-tail swimbaits in the 4 to 5-inch range, fished on light jig heads and walked over the tops of the submerged rock piles off Esker Point and through the gut between Fishers Island and the mainland, drawing occasional fish but nothing consistent yet. That bite usually wakes up hard once water temps drop into the low 60s, which we're not at.

Fluke are winding down, as expected this time of year. A few keeper-class fish are still coming off the sand edges in Little Narragansett Bay and around the Mystic River mouth on white Gulp paired with a bucktail, but the bite has thinned noticeably from August, and most of the boats that were dedicated fluke trips a month ago have shifted their attention to the surface stuff. Black sea bass remain the steady mixed-bag option — the reef structure off Fishers Island and the deeper rock edges outside the breakwater are still holding fish willing to eat squid strips and clam on a standard high-low rig, and that fishery should hold up fine through the month even as everything else around it changes character.

Tautog season hasn't opened yet in these waters, so that rock-pile blackfish bite everyone's been eyeing all summer stays off-limits for a few more weeks — but the boulder fields that will hold tog in October are the same ones currently loaded with albie and bonito activity, which tells you something about how good that structure is going to fish once the calendar turns.

For the next several days, expect more of the same pattern: scattered albie and bonito activity on the tide changes, particularly the last two hours of the incoming when bait gets pushed hard against the rocks at Ram Island and the eastern breakwater face, with bunker-bass action holding steady at Watch Hill Reef. The real swing point is the new moon on the 10th. If the bait stays concentrated and the wind stays out of the south rather than kicking up out of the northeast, that's when this corridor should go from feeder pods to fish that stay up. Worth keeping the light rods rigged and ready — this is the window where Fishers Island Sound earns its reputation.
